title: Box Office Shock: Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Posts 19‑Year Low, ‘Verity’ Claims Top Spot【Deadline】
body:
Warner Bros.’ latest high‑budget, auteur‑driven thriller **“Digger,”** starring Tom Cruise, opened to a modest $8 million domestic haul this weekend, marking the actor’s weakest opening in nearly two decades. The film’s performance was buoyed by solid attendance in several regional markets, but it was eclipsed nationally by the psychological drama **“Verity,”** which seized the top spot at the box office.

“Digger” managed to generate $8 million across a wide release, but the figure falls short of expectations for a Cruise vehicle, especially given the film’s sizable production budget and extensive marketing push. The opening represents the lowest debut for the star since the 2007 drama *Lions for Lambs*, which earned $6.7 million on a considerably smaller scale. Industry analysts point to a combination of factors – including the film’s niche, “very original” storytelling approach, a crowded release slate, and tepid critical buzz – as contributors to the underwhelming turnout.

Despite the overall softness, the movie found pockets of enthusiasm. Attendance was strongest in the South, the East, South‑Central, and Midwest regions, where audiences responded positively to the film’s blend of action and introspection. The per‑location average (PLF) data revealed that PLF screens accounted for 28 percent of the total gross, indicating that a sizable share of revenue came from premium formats such as Dolby Cinema and premium large‑format theatres, even though “Digger” did not appear in any IMAX venues. Notably, the AMC Lincoln Square location in New York City posted the highest single‑theater earnings, pulling in $36,300, a testament to the film’s appeal among urban cinephiles.

The weekend’s box‑office hierarchy was dominated by **“Verity,”** a low‑budget thriller that leveraged strong word‑of‑mouth and a compelling narrative to outpace the star‑powered “Digger.” “Verity” demonstrates the growing volatility of the market, where modestly budgeted films can eclipse high‑profile releases when they resonate more effectively with audiences. The contrast underscores a shifting landscape in which star power alone no longer guarantees box‑office dominance, especially when competing against content that taps into current cultural conversations and social media momentum.

Trade observers also highlighted the strategic implications for Warner Bros. The studio’s gamble on a “very original, very expensive” project underscores an ongoing tension between artistic ambition and commercial viability. While “Digger” showcases Cruise’s willingness to experiment beyond the conventional franchise formula, the modest opening suggests that audiences may be more selective, gravitating toward stories that deliver both novelty and clear genre signposts. The absence of an IMAX release, a staple for many blockbuster openings, may have further limited the film’s revenue ceiling, as premium‑format tickets often boost opening weekend numbers for big‑budget titles.

Looking ahead, “Digger” faces a steep uphill battle to sustain momentum. Its performance in the coming weeks will hinge on whether positive word‑of‑mouth can offset the initial lukewarm reception and whether ancillary platforms—streaming, international markets, and home video—can recoup the sizable investment. Meanwhile, “Verity” is poised to capitalize on its current lead, potentially extending its run if the buzz continues. The weekend’s results serve as a reminder that the box office is increasingly driven by content relevance and audience engagement, rather than marquee names alone, and that studios may need to recalibrate their risk‑taking strategies in an environment where even the biggest stars cannot guarantee a blockbuster opening.
